title: Increased overall mortality and liver-related mortality in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
text_summary: 研究利用NHANES III及其死亡登记联结资料，在美国一般人群中评估NAFLD的全因和肝病相关死亡风险。12,822名受试者中817名符合NAFLD定义，中位随访8.7年；校正人口学和代谢危险因素后，NAFLD仍与较高全因死亡和约9倍肝病相关死亡风险相关。心血管疾病和恶性肿瘤是主要死因，肝病与脑血管病并列NAFLD人群第三位死因，提示随访需同时重视心血管风险和肝病进展。
text:
Increased overall mortality and liver-related mortality
in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease q
Janus P. Ong 1,2, Angela Pitts 3, Zobair M. Younossi 1,2,*
1Center for Liver Diseases, Inova Fairfax Hospital, 3289 Woodburn Road, Suite 375, Annandale, VA 22003, USA
2Outcomes Research Program, Inova Health System, Falls Church, VA, USA
3RTI International, Research Triangle Park, NC, USA
Background/Aims: The natural history of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) remains to be deﬁned. We con-
ducted a study to determine the overall and liver-related mortality of NAFLD in the general US population.
Methods: In this study, the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III) and NHANES
III-Linked Mortality File were used. Adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for overall and liver-related mortality were calculated
for NAFLD using persons without liver disease as reference. Causes of death were determined.
Results: After a median follow-up of 8.7 years, 80 persons with NAFLD and 1453 without liver disease died. Older age,
male gender, non-Hispanic white race, lower educational level, lower income, higher BMI, presence of hypertension, dia-
betes mellitus, or metabolic syndrome were signiﬁcantly ( p < 0.05) associated with overall mortality. Persons with
NAFLD had higher overall mortality [HR 1.038 (95% CI 1.036–1.041), P < 0.0001] and liver-related mortality [HR
9.32 (95% CI 9.21–9.43), P < 0.0001]. Liver disease was the third leading cause of death among persons with NAFLD
after cardiovascular disease and malignancy.
Conclusions: NAFLD is associated with higher overall and liver-related mortality in the general US population. Liver
disease is a signiﬁcant cause of death among persons with NAFLD.

Keywords: NAFLD; NASH; Liver-related mortality; USA
1. Introduction
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is one
of the most common causes of chronic liver disease
in the United States with a prevalence estimated to
be as high as 34% in one study [1,2]. Patients with
NAFLD can develop progressive liver disease leading
to end-stage liver disease and hepatocellular carci-
noma [2]. The natural history of NAFLD however
remains to be deﬁned in the general United States
population [2]. In a community-based cohort study,
persons with NAFLD had a higher mortality rate
compared to the general population. Liver disease
was the third most common cause of death in those
with NAFLD while it was the thirteenth leading cause
of death in the general population [3]. This study
however may not reﬂect the general population of
the United States. We set out to determine the impact
of NAFLD on overall and liver-related mortality in
the general United States population and to determine
the causes of mortality in persons with NAFLD using
a population-based sample.

2. Methods
2.1. NHANES III linked mortality ﬁle
The current study utilizes data from the Third National Health and
Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III) and the NHANES III
Linked Mortality File. NHANES III was a survey conducted by the
NCHS in the period 1988–1994 to obtain national statistics on the
health and nutritional status of the non-institutionalized civilian pop-
ulation by means of household interviews, standardized physical
exams, and collection and testing of blood samples in special mobile
examination centers [4]. After weighting on the basis of age, sex, level
of education, and race or ethnic group, the distribution of participants
was representative of that of the US population as a whole [4].
The NHANES III-Linked Mortality File was created by the
National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) by linking the third
National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III)
with the National Death Index (NDI) [5]. The NDI is a computerized
database of all certiﬁed deaths in the United States since 1979. All
NHANES III participants 17 years and older have mortality follow-
up until December 31, 2000. In addition to mortality status, the
NHANES III-Linked Mortality File contains dates of death as well
as causes of death [5]. The NHANES III-Linked Mortality File pro-
vides a unique opportunity to evaluate the natural history of NAFLD
in the general United States population.
2.2. Study population ( Fig. 1 )
All adult participants (17+ years old) were included in the study
cohort. Those who did not have data on causes of liver disease (i.e.,
AST, ALT, testing for Hepatitis B or C, alcohol use, and transferrin
saturation) and those who do not have data on age, gender, race, edu-
cation, income, hypertension, diabetes, body mass index, waist circum-
ference, blood pressure, blood glucose, triglycerides, and HDL were
excluded.
2.3. Deﬁnitions
Elevated serum aminotransferases were deﬁned as ALT > 40 U/L
or AST > 37 in men or ALT or AST > 31 U/L in women.
Diabetes mellitus was deﬁned as ongoing use of oral hypoglycemic
agents and/or insulin or if their fasting plasma glucose level was
126 mg/dL or greater.
Hypertension was deﬁned as ongoing use of antihypertensive med-
ications or if their systolic BP is 140 mmHg or greater or their diastolic
BP is 90 mmHg or greater.
Metabolic syndrome was deﬁned as the presence of three out of the
following features according to the National Cholesterol Education
Program (NCEP) deﬁnition [6]:
A. Waist circumference greater than 102 cm in men or greater than
88 cm in women.
B. Triglyceride level P 150 mg/dL.
C. HDL less than 40 mg/dL in men or less than 50 mg/dL in
women.
D. Systolic BP P130 mmHg or diastolic BP P85 mmHg.
E. Fasting plasma glucose level P110 mg/dL.
For the purposes of this study, persons with elevated serum amino-
transferases in the absence of signiﬁcant alcohol use, elevated transfer-
rin saturation, positivity for either HCV-RNA or HBsAg were
considered to have NAFLD.
For the purposes of this study, those with normal serum amino-
transferases in the absence of signiﬁcant alcohol use, elevated transfer-
rin saturation, positivity for either HCV-RNA or HBsAg were
considered as not having liver disease.
Liver-related death was deﬁned as death associated with cirrhosis
or its complications using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes ( Table 1 ). Causes
of death were coded according to the 9th revision of the International
Statistical Classiﬁcation of Diseases, Injuries, and Causes of Death
(ICD-9) for deaths occurring up to 1998 and according to the 10th
revision (ICD-10) for those occurring from 1999 onwards [5].
3. Analysis
Baseline characteristics were described and tabulated.
Hazard ratios for overall mortality were calculated for
each baseline characteristic. Adjusted hazard ratios for
overall mortality and for liver-related mortality were
calculated for NAFLD using persons with no liver dis-
ease as reference. Cox proportional hazards model was
used. SAS (Cary, NC) was used for the analysis. The

4. Results
The initial cohort considered for this study included
12,822 persons from NHANES III and NHANES III
Linked Mortality Files ( Fig. 1 ). Among these partici-
pants, 817 persons (6.4%) fulﬁlled our deﬁnition of
NAFLD, 10,468 persons (81.6%) did not have evidence
of liver disease, and 1537 persons (12%) had signiﬁcant
alcohol use, elevated transferrin saturation, or positivity
for either HCV-RNA or HBsAg. This last group of
patients with chronic liver disease was excluded from
further analysis.
Baseline characteristics NAFLD and controls are
shown in Table 2 . Persons with NAFLD were younger,
more likely to be male, less likely to be white, have lower
income, have less education, and more likely to be
obese, have hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or meta-
bolic syndrome ( Table 2 ).
4.1. Overall and liver-related mortality
There were 1533 persons who died on follow-up.
Among these, 80 were persons with NAFLD and 1453
were persons with no liver disease. The median duration
of follow-up was 8.7 years for the entire cohort, 8.4
years for persons with NAFLD, and 8.8 years for per-
sons with no liver disease.
Older age, male gender, non-Hispanic white race,
lower educational level, lower income, higher BMI,
and the presence of hypertension, diabetes mellitus,
or the metabolic syndrome were signiﬁcantly associ-
ated with mortality (Hazard Ratios for Overall Mor-
tality are listed in Table 2 ). Overall mortality was
signiﬁcantly higher in persons with NAFLD after
adjusting for potential confounding variables ( Table
3, Fig. 2 ).
Furthermore, liver-related mortality was likewise sig-
niﬁcantly higher among persons with NAFLD after
adjusting for potential confounding variables ( Table 3 ,
Fig. 2 ).
4.2. Causes of death
Cardiovascular diseases and malignancy were the
leading causes of death among persons with NAFLD
(Table 4 ). Liver disease tied with cerebrovascular
diseases as the third leading cause of death among
persons with NAFLD. On the other hand, liver disease
was only the 11th leading cause of death in persons
without liver disease. All the liver-related deaths among
persons with NAFLD were due to cirrhosis or chronic
liver disease.

5. Discussion
The natural history of NAFLD in the general United
States population remains to be deﬁned [2,7]. Previous
studies have evaluated cohorts of persons with NAFLD
either from tertiary care referral centers [8] or from com-
munity-based studies [3]. In the present study, we uti-
lized a large population-based sample to assess the risk
of death in persons with NAFLD compared to those
without NAFLD or liver disease. After adjusting for
important confounders, persons with NAFLD had a
higher risk of dying compared to those without NAFLD
or liver disease. This is similar to the ﬁndings from two
very recent studies [3,9]. Using a community-based sam-
ple, Adams et al. demonstrated a lower survival among
persons with NAFLD compared to the general popula-
tion [3]. In a diﬀerent study, Ekstedt et al. showed that
persons with NAFLD, in particular those with the sub-
type of NASH, had a reduced survival when compared
with a matched reference population [9]. Both these
studies however may not necessarily reﬂect the general
United States population. The current study utilized
the NHANES III, which reﬂects the non-institutional-
ized population of the United States and likely repre-
sents the general population more closely.
The ﬁndings in this study diﬀer from those of another
study where patients with NAFLD had similar survival
to the general Danish population [10]. This can be
explained by the fact that the population in the Danish
study consisted wholly of patients with simple steatosis
while the present study likely included patients reﬂecting
the entire spectrum of NAFLD, from simple steatosis to
non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). It is believed that
simple steatosis is not associated with progressive liver
disease while those with NASH can have a progressive
course [2]. This is best illustrated in the study by Ekstedt
et al. where patients with NASH had reduced survival
and those with simple steatosis did not when compared
with the reference population [9].
The present study also showed that persons with
NAFLD have a higher likelihood of dying of a liver-
related complication compared to those without
NAFLD or liver disease. This risk was independent of
obesity or the presence of diabetes mellitus, the latter
has been associated with higher rates of liver-related
deaths among persons with NAFLD [11].
Among the various causes of death, cardiovascular
disease and malignancy remain to be the most important
causes of death in persons with NAFLD in the present

study. This essentially conﬁrms the ﬁndings of previ-
ously published cohort studies [3,8,9]. The fact that car-
diovascular disease remains the leading cause of death
among persons with NAFLD is not surprising, as
NAFLD is now believed to the hepatic manifestation
of the metabolic syndrome [12]. Furthermore, there is
an increasing body of literature that suggests that
NAFLD is an independent predictor of cardiovascular
morbidity and mortality [13]. Like previous studies, liver
disease is an important cause of mortality after cardio-
vascular disease and malignancy among persons with
NAFLD in this study. None of the patients with
NAFLD in this study, who died, had hepatocellular car-
cinoma. In the study by Adams et al. [3], one of seven
liver-related deaths was due to hepatocellular carcinoma
and one of two liver-related deaths in the study of
Ekstedt et al. [9] was due to a hepatocellular carcinoma.
The relationship between NAFLD and cancer has been
evaluated with retrospectively gathered data and
requires further investigation with prospective studies
[14,15].
A limitation of our study is the use of elevated serum
aminotransferases (in the absence of any other liver dis-
ease) as a marker of NAFLD, which may underestimate
the true prevalence of NAFLD in the sample. However,
the impact of NAFLD on mortality remains signiﬁcant
despite the possibility of misclassifying persons with
NAFLD into the group without NAFLD or liver dis-
ease. Moreover, this deﬁnition of NAFLD has been
employed in many published epidemiological studies of
NAFLD [16–19]. The strengths of our study include
the use of a population-based sample, the relatively long
duration of follow-up, and the low rates of unmatched
records in the NHANES III Linked Mortality File.
In conclusion, we report that persons with NAFLD
are at signiﬁcantly higher risk of mortality, including
liver-related mortality. This study extends the results
of previous cohort studies to the general United States
population and includes the impact of NAFLD on
liver-related mortality. Cardiovascular disease remains
the leading cause of death among persons with NAFLD
highlighting the need to pay attention to the cardiovas-
cular risk proﬁle in persons with NAFLD who are likely
to have multiple risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

第2页：双栏方法页说明NHANES III死亡联结资料、研究人群、NAFLD及死亡原因定义和统计分析；图1为13,970人筛选至12,822人并分组的流程图。
第3页：表1列出肝硬化及其并发症的ICD-9和ICD-10代码；表2比较NAFLD与无肝病人群的基线特征并给出总体死亡风险比，正文报告死亡结果。
第4页：表3给出校正后的全因和肝病相关死亡风险比；图2比较两组全因及肝病死亡风险，表4列出具体死亡原因，正文进入讨论。
第5页：双栏讨论、结论、致谢和参考文献页，分析NAFLD总体及肝病死亡增加的意义、局限和临床随访重点，无新增图表。
